title: Vector
one_line: A vector is an ordered list of numbers that adds coordinate by coordinate and scales by a constant, so lists of numbers and arrows obey exactly the same arithmetic.
check: Q: Add u = (3, 1) and v = (1, 2). A: (4, 3), which is also the arrow from the origin to the head of v laid at the head of u.

title: Inner product
one_line: The inner product multiplies matching entries of two vectors and sums them, and it equals the product of the two lengths times the cosine of the angle between them.
check: Q: What is the inner product of two vectors at right angles? A: Exactly zero, because cos 90 degrees is zero.

title: Norm of a vector
one_line: The Euclidean length of a vector is the square root of its inner product with itself, so a vector with n equal entries of size mu has length mu times the square root of n.
check: Q: A vector has 400 entries each equal to 0.005 in absolute value. What is its 2-norm? A: 0.005 times sqrt(400) = 0.1.

title: Orthogonality
one_line: Two vectors are orthogonal when their inner product is exactly zero, which is the algebraic statement that they sit at a right angle and neither carries any component of the other.
check: Q: If B transpose times x equals the zero vector, what does that say about x? A: x is orthogonal to every column of B at once.

title: Span
one_line: The span of a set of vectors is every vector you can build from them by scaling and adding, which is a flat sheet through the origin whose dimension counts the independent directions.
check: Q: Two vectors in the plane are scalar multiples of each other. What is the dimension of their span? A: One, a line, not two.

title: Subspace
one_line: A subspace is a set closed under addition and scaling, so it is a flat sheet through the origin, and every span is a subspace of some dimension inside a bigger space.
check: Q: Must a subspace contain the origin? A: Yes, because scaling any of its vectors by zero has to stay inside it.

title: Matrix as a linear map
one_line: An n by m matrix is a machine that eats a vector of length m and returns a vector of length n, so columns match the input and rows match the output.
check: Q: A loadings matrix B is 3000 by 60. What length vector does it consume and what length does it emit? A: It consumes 60 factor returns and emits 3000 asset returns.

title: Column space
one_line: The column space of a matrix is the span of its columns, and since any product Bf is a weighted sum of those columns, Bf can never leave the column space whatever f is.
check: Q: With 3000 assets and 60 factors, how many of the 3000 directions can the systematic return reach? A: Sixty, so the systematic part is trapped on a 60 dimensional sheet.

title: Rank of a matrix
one_line: The rank of a matrix is the dimension of its column space, meaning the number of genuinely independent columns, and a sample covariance from T observations has rank at most T.
check: Q: A 252 day sample covariance matrix on 440 names has what rank at most? A: 251, so it is singular and cannot be inverted.

title: Orthogonal complement
one_line: The orthogonal complement of a subspace is every vector at right angles to all of it, and in n dimensions a rank m subspace leaves n minus m complementary directions.
check: Q: With 3000 assets and 60 factors, how many directions lie in the orthogonal complement of the factor sheet? A: 2940, which is 98 percent of the space.

title: Orthonormal basis
one_line: A set of vectors is orthonormal when every pair is orthogonal and every vector has unit length, so each contribution can be read off with no cross terms and the Gram matrix is the identity.
check: Q: If U has orthonormal columns, what is U transpose times U? A: The identity matrix, which is why inverses vanish from projection formulas built on U.

title: Gram matrix
one_line: The Gram matrix X transpose X records how much each column of X overlaps every other column, and inverting it is exactly what undoes the double counting in a regression.
check: Q: What does a large off diagonal entry of the Gram matrix mean? A: Two predictors overlap heavily, so they are not independent sources of information.

title: Projection onto a subspace
one_line: The projection of a vector onto a subspace is the closest point of that subspace, equivalently the unique point whose leftover is perpendicular to the whole subspace.
check: Q: Two conditions define the same projection point. Name them. A: Closest point of the sheet, and residual perpendicular to every direction in the sheet.

title: Normal equations
one_line: Requiring the residual to be perpendicular to every column of X gives X transpose times (y minus X beta) equals zero, whose solution is beta hat equals (X transpose X) inverse X transpose y.
check: Q: What single geometric demand produces the normal equations? A: The residual must be orthogonal to every column of X, not merely to the fitted vector.

title: Hat matrix
one_line: The hat matrix H equals X times (X transpose X) inverse times X transpose, the operator that casts the shadow of y onto the column space of X and so puts the hat on y.
check: Q: What does I minus H do to a vector? A: It returns the residual, which is why it is called the residual maker.

title: Idempotence
one_line: An operator is idempotent when applying it twice changes nothing beyond applying it once, which is exactly the picture that the shadow of a shadow is the same shadow.
check: Q: State idempotence for the hat matrix in symbols. A: H squared equals H.

title: Trace of a projection
one_line: The trace of an orthogonal projection matrix equals the dimension of the subspace it projects onto, so it counts how many directions the fit has spent.
check: Q: A nine point fit on two columns has what trace for H and for I minus H? A: 2 and 7, which is where degrees of freedom come from.

title: Pythagorean decomposition
one_line: Because the projection and the residual meet at a right angle, their squared lengths add to the squared length of the original vector, so variances add while volatilities do not.
check: Q: Factor volatility is 141,146 dollars and idiosyncratic volatility 181,580. What is total volatility? A: About 229,986 dollars, not their sum of 322,726.

title: Eigenvalue equation
one_line: A vector v is an eigenvector of a matrix when the matrix only stretches it, so that Sigma times v equals lambda times v with lambda the eigenvalue for that direction.
check: Q: Write the eigenvalue equation for a covariance matrix. A: Sigma v equals lambda v, with v a nonzero vector.

title: Eigendecomposition of a symmetric matrix
one_line: A symmetric positive semidefinite matrix has real nonnegative eigenvalues and an orthonormal set of eigenvectors, so it can be written as U times a diagonal matrix times U transpose.
check: Q: Write a symmetric positive semidefinite Sigma in eigen form. A: Sigma = U S U transpose with U orthonormal and S diagonal and nonnegative.

title: Rayleigh quotient
one_line: The ratio of x transpose A x to x transpose x can never exceed the largest eigenvalue of the symmetric matrix A, and it attains that maximum at the top eigenvector.
check: Q: Measured Rayleigh quotient is 0.086669 and the operator norm is 0.158270. Is that consistent? A: Yes, the quotient must be at or below the largest eigenvalue.

title: Operator norm
one_line: The operator norm of a matrix is the largest factor by which it can stretch any vector, and for a diagonal matrix that is simply the largest diagonal entry.
check: Q: What is the operator norm of a diagonal idiosyncratic covariance matrix? A: The variance of the single noisiest stock, footnoted near 40 percent annualised for US equities.

title: Condition number
one_line: The condition number is the ratio of largest to smallest eigenvalue, and it bounds how much a relative error in a matrix can be amplified in its inverse.
check: Q: A matrix has largest eigenvalue 97.32 and smallest 0.00544. What is its condition number? A: About 17,899, so a one percent input error can become a 17,899 percent output error.

title: Singular value decomposition
one_line: Every matrix factors as U times S times V transpose, which reads as a rotation, then a stretch of each axis by its own singular value, then another rotation.
check: Q: Which of the three SVD factors is the only one that changes shape? A: The diagonal stretch S; the two rotations only change orientation.

title: Frobenius norm
one_line: The Frobenius norm squares every entry of a matrix, sums them and takes the root, so it is the ordinary Euclidean length of the matrix flattened into one long vector.
check: Q: A difference matrix flattens to (0.04, 0.08, 0.00, -0.09). What is its Frobenius norm? A: 0.1269, the ordinary length of that list.

title: Eckart-Young theorem
one_line: Truncating the SVD at the largest m singular values gives the best possible rank m approximation in any unitarily invariant norm, and the leftover error equals the discarded singular values.
check: Q: What is the squared Frobenius error of the best rank m approximation? A: The sum of the squared singular values you discarded, an identity rather than a bound.

title: Matrix square root
one_line: Square rooting the eigenvalues of a symmetric positive semidefinite matrix gives a matrix that squares back to it, which is the object that whitens or colours a random vector.
check: Q: If xi is standard Gaussian, what is the covariance of Omega to the half times xi? A: Exactly Omega, because covariance eats the transform twice.

title: Matrix determinant lemma
one_line: For any two vectors the determinant of the identity plus a rank one update a nu transpose equals one plus nu transpose a, so the update is singular exactly when that inner product is minus one.
check: Q: When is I + a nu transpose singular? A: Exactly when nu transpose a equals minus one.

title: One norm versus two norm inequality
one_line: The 1-norm of an n vector never exceeds the square root of n times its 2-norm, with equality exactly when every coordinate has the same size.
check: Q: Every entry of an n vector has size mu. Compare its 1-norm and 2-norm. A: The 1-norm is n mu and the 2-norm is sqrt(n) mu, so the ratio is exactly sqrt(n).

title: Convexity and concavity
one_line: A function is concave if it bends downward so that it lies above every chord, and convex if it bends upward so that it lies below every chord.
check: Q: Is 1 over x convex or concave on the positive numbers? A: Convex, which is why averaging reciprocals lands above the reciprocal of the average.

title: Jensen's inequality
one_line: For a concave function the expectation of the function is at most the function of the expectation, with equality only where the function is affine on the support of the variable.
check: Q: A fair coin pays minus 40 percent or plus 80 percent. Compare log(1+E[r]) with E[log(1+r)]. A: 0.182 against 0.038, a Jensen gap of 0.144.

title: Taylor expansion
one_line: A smooth function can be written near a point as a constant plus a slope term plus a curvature term plus corrections that shrink near the point and grow away from it.
check: Q: Expanding minus exp(-gx) around zero, what is the first term the quadratic approximation discards? A: The cubic term (gx) cubed over 6.

title: Logarithm as a group isomorphism
one_line: The logarithm maps the multiplicative group of positive reals onto the additive real line, turning products into sums exactly and invertibly, which is its defining equation rather than a convenience.
check: Q: Why is exp of the sum of log returns exactly the compound return? A: Because log is invertible and turns the product into a sum, so the round trip is an identity, not an approximation.

title: Basis change
one_line: Replacing X by X times an invertible matrix Q leaves every fitted value unchanged while changing every coefficient, so a coefficient is never a basis free statement.
check: Q: Under a change of basis the fit stayed identical to 2.1e-14 but the estimate moved from (0.343, 0.507) to what kind of thing? A: A different coefficient pair, (0.095, 0.153), describing the same predictions.

title: Lagrangian
one_line: The Lagrangian adds to the objective a multiplier times the slack in each constraint, so that setting its gradient to zero characterises the constrained stationary points.
check: Q: Differentiate w'Sigma w + lambda(1 - w'w) and set it to zero. A: 2 Sigma w minus 2 lambda w equals zero, which is the eigenvalue equation.

title: Random variable
one_line: A random variable is a labelled slot that has not been filled yet, together with how likely each possible value is, and you get exactly one draw from it per occasion.
check: Q: Is Monday's crow count a random variable before or after you look? A: Before; after you look it is a fact, and the randomness lived in the unfilled slot.

title: Probability as a repeated experiment
one_line: A probability is the fraction of imaginary re-runs of the same occasion that produce the outcome, so it is a property of the occasion considered as repeatable and never of the single day you lived.
check: Q: Can you observe p by watching harder on Monday? A: No, p lives down the column of imaginary re-runs and you only ever see one entry of it.

title: Bernoulli distribution
one_line: A Bernoulli variable takes value one with probability p and zero otherwise, so its whole distribution is two bars, with mean p and variance p times one minus p.
check: Q: At which p is a Bernoulli variance largest, and what is it? A: At p equals one half, where the variance is 0.25.

title: Independence
one_line: Two variables are independent when knowing one changes nothing about the other, which is used for exactly one thing: turning a joint probability into a product.
check: Q: What single algebraic step does an independence assumption buy? A: It lets the probability of a whole sequence be written as the product of the per day probabilities.

title: Identically distributed
one_line: Identically distributed means every occasion is drawn from the same law, which is a relabelling permission that converts many variables with one draw each into one variable with many draws.
check: Q: Without the identical distribution claim, how many observations do you have per unknown? A: Exactly one, forever, and no amount of extra data collection helps.

title: Independent and identically distributed
one_line: The iid assumption is the pair of separate claims that occasions do not influence each other and that they share one law, and only the second is what licenses pooling.
check: Q: A territorial crow makes tomorrow depend on today but the long run rate settles at 0.40 every day. Which claim broke? A: Independence broke; identical distribution still holds.

title: Binomial distribution
one_line: Adding n independent Bernoulli trials gives a count with probability C(n,k) times p to the k times one minus p to the n minus k, with mean np and variance np(1-p).
check: Q: With n = 20 and p = 0.35, where does the binomial peak and why? A: At k = np = 7, where the rise in the number of arrangements stops outrunning the fall in per arrangement probability.

title: Binomial coefficient
one_line: The binomial coefficient counts how many orderings produce the same total, and it appears only because a count is a bundle of outcomes you decided not to tell apart.
check: Q: Does dropping C(n,k) move the maximum likelihood estimate of p? A: No, it contains no p, so the argmax is 0.35 with or without it, but the quoted probability is wrong by a factor of 77,520.

title: Expectation
one_line: The expectation of a variable is the long run average of its values weighted by their probabilities, and it passes through sums and constant multiples always, with no conditions attached.
check: Q: Does E[aX + bY] = aE[X] + bE[Y] require independence? A: No, linearity of expectation holds always.

title: Variance
one_line: Variance is the expected squared deviation from the mean, squared so deviations cannot cancel and so that independent contributions add, at the cost of living in squared units.
check: Q: Why take a square root at the end? A: To return to the units of the variable, giving the standard deviation, which is what everyone calls volatility.

title: Covariance
one_line: Covariance is the expected product of the two centred deviations, and it is the term that appears when the variance of a sum is expanded.
check: Q: What is the covariance of a linear map of a random vector? A: cov(B xi) = B Omega B transpose, the matrix acting once from each side.

title: Correlation
one_line: Correlation is covariance divided by the two standard deviations, so it lies between minus one and one and measures straight line agreement and nothing else.
check: Q: What kind of relationship is correlation blind to? A: Every nonlinear one, including a deterministic relation such as Y equals X squared with X symmetric.

title: Variance of a sum
one_line: The variance of a sum equals the sum of the variances plus twice the sum of the covariances, so variances add only when the cross terms vanish.
check: Q: T uncorrelated daily returns each with volatility sigma. What is the standard deviation of the sum? A: sigma times the square root of T, because it is variances that add, not standard deviations.

title: Uncorrelated is not independent
one_line: Zero correlation only rules out straight line dependence, so a process built as r_t = h_t epsilon_t is exactly uncorrelated while being enormously dependent through the size of past moves.
check: Q: A GARCH series had correlation 0.002 between consecutive returns and 0.207 between consecutive absolute returns. What does that show? A: Uncorrelated in sign yet strongly dependent in size.

title: Standard error of a sample mean
one_line: The variance of an average of n independent draws is the single draw variance divided by n, so the standard error falls like one over the square root of n.
check: Q: A hundred times the data buys how much precision? A: Ten times, because the error falls like one over the square root of n, a slope of minus one half on log axes.

title: Law of large numbers
one_line: The average of many independent draws converges to the true mean provided that mean exists, which is why estimation works at all and why it silently fails when it does not.
check: Q: Five runs of 200,000 draws from a Student t with one degree of freedom finished at minus 5.45, minus 0.93, plus 1.20, plus 0.15 and minus 0.37. Why? A: The mean does not exist, so there is nothing to converge to.

title: Central limit theorem
one_line: The standardised sum of many independent draws with finite variance approaches a Gaussian, so the bell is a residue of adding rather than an assumption anyone made.
check: Q: Sums of exponential draws had measured skewness 1.98, 1.41, 0.89, 0.37 at n = 1, 2, 5, 30. What exact law is that? A: Skewness equals 2 over the square root of n.

title: Gaussian distribution
one_line: The Gaussian is the limiting law of standardised sums, the maximum entropy law given a known mean and variance, and the unique error law making the arithmetic mean the most probable value.
check: Q: Why is the Gaussian kurtosis exactly 3? A: It is the value of the integral of z to the fourth against the density, which returns 3 rather than being a convention.

title: Moments
one_line: The k-th moment is the average of x to the k, chosen historically because it is trivially computable from data, and it summarises but does not always identify a distribution.
check: Q: Do the moments determine the distribution? A: Only when the moment generating function is finite near zero; the lognormal fails that and shares every moment with a rippled twin.

title: Centered versus uncentered second moment
one_line: The uncentered second moment equals the variance plus the squared mean, so when the mean is tiny relative to the spread the two coincide and no mean has to be subtracted.
check: Q: Daily equity mean is 0.04 percent and volatility 1.2 percent. What share of E[r squared] is the mean? A: About one part in a thousand, since (sigma/mu) squared is 900.

title: Skewness
one_line: Skewness is the average cubed standardised deviation, so it measures which tail is stretched by distance rather than which side is crowded, and it is the first free descriptor of shape.
check: Q: A lottery loses one dollar with probability 0.999 and wins 999 with probability 0.001. What is its skewness sign? A: Strongly positive, plus 31.58, even though 99.9 percent of outcomes sit below the mean.

title: Kurtosis
one_line: Kurtosis is the average fourth standardised power, which weights a five sigma day 625 times a one sigma day, so it is a statement about tail dominance and about how few days set the number.
check: Q: For a fat tailed sample of 100,000 draws, what share of the kurtosis came from the ten largest observations? A: About 20 percent, against 0.95 percent for a Gaussian.

title: Power law tail
one_line: A power law tail has exceedance probability falling like a constant times x to the minus alpha, which plots as a straight line on log log axes rather than curving away as a Gaussian does.
check: Q: How do you read a tail index off a survival plot? A: Fit the slope of the straight region on log log axes; the slope is minus alpha.

title: Tail index
one_line: The tail index alpha of a power law is not a description of thickness but a cutoff: it says which moments exist, and how fast the once in N event grows with N.
check: Q: How large is the one in a million event under alpha = 4, 3 and 2? A: About 32, 100 and 1000 sigma, against 4.8 sigma for a Gaussian.

title: Existence of a moment
one_line: A moment of order k is finite if and only if k is below the tail index, so a fat tail does not make a moment large, it makes the moment fail to exist.
sources: Four Numbers and What They Threw Away (https://claude.ai/code/artifact/0b20a92e-dc03-4b4c-aa3e-0a8a0c320608)
check: Q: With alpha about 4, which of variance, skewness and kurtosis are safe? A: Variance comfortably, skewness marginally, kurtosis right on the boundary and nothing above it.

title: Poisson distribution
one_line: The Poisson is the binomial limit with many trials each rare, holding the expected count lambda fixed, and having collapsed two parameters into one it must have variance equal to mean.
check: Q: What single falsifiable prediction does a Poisson make with nowhere to hide? A: Variance equals mean, so the ratio of the two must be exactly one.

title: Fano factor
one_line: The Fano factor is the ratio of variance to mean, exactly one for any Poisson, so a measured value far from one refuses the model on its own prediction with no rival named.
check: Q: The crow year had mean 14.29 and variance 80.6. What is the Fano factor and the verdict? A: 5.64, so the Poisson is refused by a factor of five and a half.

title: Law of total variance
one_line: The variance of a variable equals the expected conditional variance plus the variance of the conditional mean, so treating a moving parameter as fixed adds exactly the second term.
check: Q: A Poisson count whose rate is itself random has what variance? A: E[lambda] plus Var(lambda); the second term is the entire excess over Poisson.

title: Mixture distribution
one_line: A mixture flips a coin and draws from one of several laws, which keeps the ingredients visible as separate lumps and is the operation that manufactures fat tails.
check: Q: Mix 88 percent N(0, 0.72 squared) with 12 percent N(0, 2.2 squared). What kurtosis results? A: 8.5, from two Gaussians and no fat tailed ingredient at all.

title: Mixing is not adding
one_line: Adding independent variables preserves the bell by the central limit theorem, while mixing distributions produces humps and fat tails belonging to none of the parts.
check: Q: Two Gaussians at minus 2 and plus 2 are added, then mixed. What kurtosis does each produce? A: 3.003 when added, still a bell, and 1.721 with two humps when mixed.

title: Negative binomial distribution
one_line: Giving a Poisson rate its own gamma distribution and integrating it out produces the negative binomial, which is the standard model of an overdispersed count.
check: Q: A gamma mixed Poisson gave P(X = 0) of 0.1248 against 0.0496 for a plain Poisson of the same mean. Which model is which? A: The mixture is the negative binomial, with Fano 2.004 against 1.000.

title: Exponential distribution
one_line: The waiting time until the next Poisson event has survival function exp(minus lambda t), a law that also follows from memorylessness alone with no mention of Poisson.
check: Q: Give two independent routes to the exponential. A: Zero Poisson events by time t, and the functional equation from memorylessness.

title: Memorylessness
one_line: A wait is memoryless when the chance of waiting a further t does not depend on how long you have already waited, and the only continuous laws satisfying that are exponential.
check: Q: State memorylessness in symbols. A: P(T > s + t given T > s) equals P(T > t), so S(s+t) = S(s)S(t).

title: Gamma distribution
one_line: Adding k independent exponential waits gives a gamma, whose peak lifts off zero as k grows because waiting for five events is rarely quick.
check: Q: What is a gamma with shape k equal to one? A: Exactly the exponential distribution.

title: Chi-squared distribution
one_line: A chi-squared with k degrees of freedom is the sum of k squared standard Gaussians, so it is the law of any quantity built from squares, with mean k and variance 2k.
check: Q: What is the relative noise of a chi-squared with k degrees of freedom divided by k? A: The square root of 2 over k, so 1.41 at k = 1 and 0.16 at k = 78.

title: Student's t distribution
one_line: Dividing a standard Gaussian by the square root of an independent scaled chi-squared gives Student's t, a Gaussian that admits it does not know its variance, with tail index equal to its degrees of freedom.
check: Q: What is the tail index of a Student t with 3 degrees of freedom, and does its kurtosis exist? A: Alpha equals 3, so the fourth moment does not exist.

title: Lognormal distribution
one_line: A product of many small independent positive factors has a Gaussian logarithm, so the lognormal is the Gaussian written in a multiplicative coordinate and is the law of a compounding price.
check: Q: Why is the 1 over y factor in the lognormal density there? A: It is the Jacobian of the log transform, nothing more.

title: Maximum entropy principle
one_line: Among all laws satisfying your constraints, choose the one that assumes least beyond them, and the famous distributions fall out one by one as answers to specific confessions of ignorance.
check: Q: Which law is maximum entropy given a known mean and variance on the whole line? A: The Gaussian, with entropy 1.4189 which is half the log of 2 pi e.

title: Characteristic function
one_line: The characteristic function is the expected value of exp(itX), a Fourier transform that always converges and determines the distribution uniquely, unlike the list of moments.
check: Q: Two densities share every moment exactly. What separates them? A: Their characteristic functions, which differ by up to 0.094.

title: Model versus estimator
one_line: A model is a recipe with knobs, data is one run of it, and an estimator is a formula that guesses a knob from data, so an estimator is itself random because the data were.
check: Q: Why must p and p hat carry different symbols? A: p is a fixed unknown knob of the world; p hat is a function of data, so it is random and it changes when you rerun the year.

title: Likelihood function
one_line: The likelihood is the same algebraic expression as the probability mass, read as a function of the parameter with the data held fixed, and it is not a probability distribution over the parameter.
check: Q: Integrate the Bernoulli likelihood over p after seeing 7 crows in 20 days. A: It comes to 1 over 21, not 1, which is why it is not a density over p.

title: Log-likelihood
one_line: The log-likelihood is the logarithm of the likelihood, taken because log is monotone so the answer does not move, because it turns products into sums, and because without it the arithmetic underflows to zero.
check: Q: At what sample size does a raw Bernoulli likelihood underflow a double? A: Around n = 1200, where it stores as exactly zero while the log-likelihood is an ordinary minus 647.

title: Maximum likelihood estimation
one_line: Maximum likelihood picks the parameter under which what actually happened was least surprising, which is a maximisation and not necessarily the solution of a derivative set to zero.
check: Q: For n uniform draws on [0, theta], what is the MLE and why does no derivative find it? A: The sample maximum; the likelihood is zero below it and decreasing above, so the optimum sits on a cliff edge.

title: Fisher information
one_line: The curvature of the log-likelihood at its maximum is the Fisher information, and the reciprocal square root of that curvature is the standard error of the estimate.
check: Q: Curvature at the peak measured minus 87.912. What standard error does that imply? A: 0.106654, the same number as the square root of p(1-p)/n.

title: Method of moments
one_line: The method of moments sets sample moments equal to model moments and solves, which needs no calculus and was the first general recipe for turning data into parameters.
check: Q: For a uniform on [0, theta], what does the method of moments give? A: Twice the sample mean, unbiased with spread 1.667 against the MLE's biased 9.230 with spread 0.714.

title: Bias of an estimator
one_line: The bias of an estimator is the gap between its average and the truth, and an unbiased estimator can still be useless because unbiasedness constrains the centre and says nothing about the spread.
check: Q: A squared return is unbiased for variance. How often does it land within 20 percent of the truth? A: About 9.8 percent of days, because its median reads only 0.45 of the truth.

title: Bias variance tradeoff
one_line: Bias and spread are separate complaints and you may trade one for the other, so a biased but tight estimator routinely beats an unbiased but wild one on total error.
check: Q: On the uniform ceiling problem, which of three estimators won on RMSE? A: The bias corrected MLE at 0.772, beating both the unbiased 1.666 and the raw MLE 1.049.

title: Rule of succession
one_line: Starting from a uniform prior and updating on data gives the posterior mean (k+1)/(n+2), which differs from maximum likelihood exactly where data are thin and agrees once data arrive.
check: Q: Zero crows in three days. What do maximum likelihood and Bayes report? A: 0.0000 and 0.2000, so likelihood declares a crow impossible forever on three days of evidence.

title: Shrinkage estimation
one_line: Shrinkage deliberately accepts bias by pulling many separate estimates toward a common target, buying a reduction in variance that is worth more when parameters are many and observations few.
check: Q: On a factor covariance from 40 observations, what did shrinking at rho = 0.1 buy and what did rho = 0.9 cost? A: It cut the realised risk penalty from 10.68 to 8.62 percent, while 0.9 pushed it to 40.4 percent.

title: Model selection
one_line: Choosing which family to fit is a different job from fitting inside one, and likelihood alone cannot do it because a family containing another can never fit worse.
check: Q: Six datasets were genuinely Poisson. How often did the negative binomial reach the higher likelihood? A: Six times out of six, which is guaranteed rather than lucky.

title: AIC and BIC
one_line: AIC and BIC keep the log-likelihood but charge rent per parameter, two per knob for AIC and log n per knob for BIC, so extra parameters have to earn their fee.
check: Q: Write AIC and BIC. A: AIC = minus 2 log L + 2k and BIC = minus 2 log L + k log n, lower being better.

title: Held-out validation
one_line: Scoring a fitted model on data it never saw removes the reward for memorising noise, and needs no formula at all.
check: Q: On the crow year the Poisson scored minus 837 held out and the negative binomial minus 631. Which wins and why is this convincing? A: The negative binomial, and it is convincing because memorised noise cannot help on unseen data.

title: Stationarity
one_line: A process is stationary when its statistical description does not depend on when you look, which is exactly the claim that licenses pooling many dates into one estimate.
sources: Four Numbers and What They Threw Away (https://claude.ai/code/artifact/0b20a92e-dc03-4b4c-aa3e-0a8a0c320608)
check: Q: What does stationarity buy that independence does not? A: Permission to pool observations across time, which is what turns one year into 365 usable draws.

title: Strict versus covariance stationarity
one_line: Covariance stationarity asks for a constant mean and finite constant variance, while strict stationarity asks only that the joint law be shift invariant, so a process can be strictly stationary with infinite variance.
sources: Three Roads to One Hidden Number (https://claude.ai/code/artifact/7933d34c-7c45-4c12-9671-be94ddc9d9a7)
check: Q: A Student t with tail index 1.5 has running sample variances ending at 724, 148, 332 and 126. Which stationarity does it have? A: Strict but not covariance stationarity.

title: Ergodicity
one_line: Ergodicity says the time average of one long path converges to the ensemble average across parallel universes, and it is strictly stronger than stationarity and the assumption that fails quietly.
check: Q: One path pooled over a year gave mean 14.29 and sd 8.98 against an ensemble 14.05 and 9.13. What does that coincidence demonstrate? A: Ergodicity, which is what licenses substituting time for parallel worlds.

title: Autocorrelation function
one_line: The autocorrelation at lag k is the correlation of a series with a copy of itself shifted k steps, and bars inside the band of plus or minus 1.96 over the root of T are indistinguishable from nothing.
check: Q: With 400 observations, where does the significance band sit? A: At plus or minus 0.098, so any bar inside it could easily be zero.

title: Markov property
one_line: A process is Markov when the future depends on the past only through the present, so the current state is a sufficient summary and no earlier history adds anything.
check: Q: Paths lined up at zero and split by whether they were rising or falling ended twelve steps later at plus 0.05 and minus 0.02. What does that say? A: The process is Markov; knowing the past bought nothing once the present was known.

title: Filtration
one_line: A filtration is the growing record of everything observable up to each time, and it exists to make precise which information a forecast is allowed to use.
check: Q: What is the difference between conditioning on the filtration and on yesterday alone? A: The first uses everything known; they coincide only for a Markov process.

title: Martingale
one_line: A martingale is a process whose best forecast of tomorrow is today, and because its increments are uncorrelated its variance can only grow, so with finite variance the only stationary martingale is a constant.
check: Q: Which of log price and return is the martingale, and which is stationary? A: Log price is the martingale and is not stationary; the return is the martingale difference and is stationary.

title: Conditional expectation as the best forecast
one_line: Under squared loss the forecast minimising expected error given x is the conditional expectation of y given x, because the cross term dies and only an unavoidable noise floor plus a squared penalty remain.
check: Q: Which two facts kill the cross term in the completed square? A: The forecast is a function of x alone, and the leftover has zero conditional mean.

title: State-space model
one_line: A state-space model pairs an evolution equation for a hidden state with an observation equation that shows it through noise, and recovering the state from observations is called filtering.
sources: Three Roads to One Hidden Number (https://claude.ai/code/artifact/7933d34c-7c45-4c12-9671-be94ddc9d9a7)
check: Q: In the plane and radar analogy, what are the two separate error sources? A: The plane genuinely moved, which is process noise, and the instrument genuinely lied, which is observation noise.

title: Kalman filter
one_line: For a linear Gaussian state-space model the optimal filter has a closed form: the new belief is the old belief plus a gain times the surprise, and the gain is a regression coefficient.
depends_on: Conditional expectation as the best forecast
sources: Three Roads to One Hidden Number (https://claude.ai/code/artifact/7933d34c-7c45-4c12-9671-be94ddc9d9a7)
check: Q: Which single fact about Gaussians does the whole derivation rest on? A: That a jointly Gaussian conditional is Gaussian with mean mu_x plus Sigma_xy Sigma_yy inverse times the surprise.

title: Kalman gain
one_line: The gain answers how much to believe today's observation against what you already thought, and its value is set by the ratio of process noise to observation noise.
sources: Three Roads to One Hidden Number (https://claude.ai/code/artifact/7933d34c-7c45-4c12-9671-be94ddc9d9a7)
check: Q: With signal to noise lambda, what is the steady state gain? A: K = (sqrt(lambda squared plus 4 lambda) minus lambda)/2, which tends to one for clean prices and zero for noisy ones.

title: Exponentially weighted moving average
one_line: An EWMA blends the newest observation with the previous estimate at a fixed weight, and it is the steady state optimal filter for a random walk state observed in noise.
sources: Three Roads to One Hidden Number (https://claude.ai/code/artifact/7933d34c-7c45-4c12-9671-be94ddc9d9a7)
check: Q: What is the half-life of an EWMA whose memory coefficient is K? A: minus log 2 over log K, so persistence 0.97 gives 23 days and 0.995 gives 138.

title: Random recursive equation
one_line: A random recursive equation is an autoregression whose coefficient is itself redrawn each period, so its fate is decided by a product of random numbers and hence by the expectation of the log, not the log of the expectation.
sources: Three Roads to One Hidden Number (https://claude.ai/code/artifact/7933d34c-7c45-4c12-9671-be94ddc9d9a7)
check: Q: A GARCH coefficient has arithmetic mean 0.985 and geometric mean 0.978. Which decides stability? A: The geometric mean, so a process whose average coefficient exceeds one can still converge almost surely.

title: Kesten's theorem
one_line: For a stationary random recursive equation the tail is a power law whose index solves E[a to the alpha over 2] equals one, so the tail index is determined by the model rather than assumed.
sources: Three Roads to One Hidden Number (https://claude.ai/code/artifact/7933d34c-7c45-4c12-9671-be94ddc9d9a7)
check: Q: Where do fitted equity GARCH parameters land on the Kesten contours? A: Squarely in the band where the implied tail index is between 4 and 6, exactly where the data live.

title: Proper scoring rule
one_line: A scoring rule is proper when the only way to minimise the expected score is to report your honest forecast, so a conservative or a flattering answer both cost you.
sources: Three Roads to One Hidden Number (https://claude.ai/code/artifact/7933d34c-7c45-4c12-9671-be94ddc9d9a7)
check: Q: Minimise log h squared plus r squared over h squared over h. A: The minimum sits exactly at h squared equal to r squared, so the loss cannot be gamed.

title: Ordinary least squares
one_line: Ordinary least squares minimises the summed squared residual, which is the projection of the outcome onto the column space of the predictors and gives beta hat from the normal equations.
depends_on: Conditional expectation as the best forecast
check: Q: Give two independent justifications that land on the identical arithmetic. A: Minimising squared loss, and maximising a Gaussian likelihood with homoskedastic independent errors.

title: Weighted least squares
one_line: Weighting each observation by the inverse of its noise variance stops the noisiest observations dominating the sum of squared residuals and gives the lowest variance unbiased linear estimate.
check: Q: An asset has four times the idiosyncratic volatility of another. What relative weight does WLS give it? A: One sixteenth, because the weight is one over the variance.

title: Frisch-Waugh-Lovell theorem
one_line: Regressing in stages gives numerically identical coefficients and residuals to the one shot regression, so a multiple regression coefficient is the simple coefficient on the part of that predictor unique to it.
check: Q: Why can a coefficient flip sign when you add a variable? A: Because the coefficient is paid only for the leftover after everything shared with the other regressors is removed.

title: Collinearity
one_line: When predictor columns nearly overlap, the smallest singular value shrinks, its square shrinks faster, and the inverse blows the coefficient variance up, so near collinearity guarantees imprecision.
check: Q: Two columns went from correlation 0.467 to 0.999. What happened to the coefficient variance? A: It rose from 1.36 to 754.5, a factor of 554, with the noise level held fixed.

title: Pseudo-inverse solution
one_line: When the design is rank deficient there are infinitely many perfect fits, and the ridgeless or pseudo-inverse answer picks the one of smallest norm, which is a criterion the data is silent about.
check: Q: Two solutions had norms 0.01015 and 0.02456 and the identical fit. What chose between them? A: The shortness criterion of the pseudo-inverse, which is not a financial reason.

title: t-statistic
one_line: A t-statistic is an estimate divided by its own standard error, so it tests whether an observed mean could plausibly have come from a distribution whose true mean is zero.
depends_on: Standard error of a sample mean
sources: Four Numbers and What They Threw Away (https://claude.ai/code/artifact/0b20a92e-dc03-4b4c-aa3e-0a8a0c320608)
check: Q: Write the t-statistic of a mean estimated from T iid observations. A: mu over sigma divided by the root of T, which equals the per period Sharpe ratio times the square root of T.

title: Newey-West estimator
one_line: The Newey-West long run variance adds tapered autocovariance terms to the contemporaneous variance, so it corrects a per period variance for the fact that risk is held for more than one period.
check: Q: An AR(1) with lag one autocorrelation 0.17 had naive daily variance 1.04e-04 against a long run 1.50e-04. How much does one lag of Newey-West recover? A: It reaches 1.22e-04, closing about two fifths of the gap.

title: Cantelli's inequality
one_line: For every distribution with a mean and a variance, the probability of falling lambda below the mean is at most sigma squared over sigma squared plus lambda squared, with a two point law attaining it exactly.
sources: Four Numbers and What They Threw Away (https://claude.ai/code/artifact/0b20a92e-dc03-4b4c-aa3e-0a8a0c320608)
check: Q: At two standard deviations below the mean, what does Cantelli promise and what does a Gaussian deliver? A: At most 20 percent against 2.3 percent, so the bound is nearly nine times loose.

title: Marchenko-Pastur law
one_line: The eigenvalues of a sample covariance of pure independent noise fill a predictable band whose upper edge is (1 plus the root of gamma) squared, where gamma is assets divided by observations.
check: Q: With gamma = 2, what top eigenvalue does pure noise produce? A: About 5.73 against a predicted edge of 5.83, even though every population eigenvalue is exactly one.

title: Eigenvalue detection threshold
one_line: A population eigenvalue below one plus the square root of gamma cannot be detected at all: its sample eigenvalue sticks at the bulk edge and its eigenvector carries no information about the truth.
check: Q: At gamma = 0.5, a real factor of strength 1.4 produced what top eigenvalue and eigenvector cosine? A: 2.90 against a bulk edge of 2.91, with cosine 0.15, so a real factor was invisible.

title: Median
one_line: The median is the fifty fifty split of a distribution, it minimises expected absolute deviation, and unlike the mean it is a counting statistic blind to how far the tail reaches.
check: Q: A single plus 200 percent day is added to 250 clean ones. What happens to the median and the mean absolute log return? A: The median rises 0.9 percent and the mean 31.8 percent.

title: Robust z-score
one_line: Dividing a security's absolute log return by the median of its own recent absolute log returns gives a scale that the outlier under test cannot inflate, unlike a standard deviation.
check: Q: Why a median and not a standard deviation in the denominator? A: Because the outlier you are hunting sits inside the sample, so a mean based scale partly disarms the detector exactly when it is needed.

title: Simple return
one_line: A simple return divides the change in price plus any dividend by the starting price, which removes the price level and makes a three dollar stock and a six hundred thousand dollar stock the same kind of object.
check: Q: What is the support of a simple return, and why does that matter? A: It lives on minus one to infinity, which is not symmetric and is the entire motivation for log returns.

title: Log return
one_line: The log return is log of one plus the simple return, the natural coordinate on the time axis because it adds across periods exactly and maps the interval minus one to infinity onto the whole real line.
check: Q: At a 1.2 percent daily move, how large is the error from using the simple return instead? A: About 0.7 basis points, invisible; at a 40 percent annual move it is about 8 percentage points.

title: Simple across assets and log across time
one_line: Simple returns add across assets through w transpose r while log returns add across time through their sum, and nothing adds across both, so mixing them silently answers a different question.
check: Q: Which coordinate does an optimizer whose objective is w transpose r require? A: Simple returns, because a portfolio log return is not the weighted sum of constituent log returns.

title: Risk-free rate
one_line: The risk-free rate is the return on an asset with negligible volatility, taken as a secured overnight rate observed from actual transactions so that an excess return is measured against a rate somebody could really transact at.
check: Q: Why did SOFR replace LIBOR as the reference here? A: SOFR is secured and transaction based, while LIBOR was unsecured and survey based, so it was a rate nobody was actually offered.

title: Excess return
one_line: Subtracting the risk-free rate from every asset return deletes the financing leg from the algebra, so a dollar neutral book and a fully invested one become the same kind of object.
sources: Four Numbers and What They Threw Away (https://claude.ai/code/artifact/0b20a92e-dc03-4b4c-aa3e-0a8a0c320608)
check: Q: At a 5 percent risk-free rate and 16 percent volatility, what does forgetting to subtract it add to a reported Sharpe ratio? A: About 0.31, for free, with no strategy attached.

title: Numeraire
one_line: The numeraire is the unit wealth is measured in, and switching it from dollars to the money market account is exactly what makes the risk-free asset identically zero rather than merely small.
check: Q: Why is a change of numeraire stronger than approximating the risk-free asset away? A: In its own units the money market account never moves, so it is exactly zero rather than approximately so.

title: Infinite divisibility
one_line: Assuming assets are infinitely divisible turns a portfolio from a point on an integer lattice into a vector in R to the n, which is what makes gradients, convex programs and every optimizer in the book legal.
check: Q: What does portfolio construction become without divisibility? A: Integer programming, which is NP hard, with no gradient and no first order condition.

title: Dollar weights
one_line: Writing the portfolio as a vector of monetary amounts rather than fractions makes profit exactly w transpose r, puts risk in dollars of daily P and L, and leaves the sum of positions free.
check: Q: Why do weights break for a market neutral book? A: Their denominator, the net market value, is zero, so dividing by it is undefined; dollars have no denominator to declare.

title: Net market value
one_line: The net market value is the signed sum of the dollar positions, which is left free by the dollar convention so that a long only, a dollar neutral and a 130 over 30 book differ only in that one number.
check: Q: Three books hold the same gross. What single quantity distinguishes long only from dollar neutral? A: The net market value, which is 100, 0 and 160 dollars respectively in the worked case.

title: Volatility drag
one_line: Geometric growth equals the arithmetic mean minus half the variance, so two assets with the same expected simple return compound at completely different rates if their volatilities differ.
check: Q: An asset has arithmetic mean 10 percent and volatility 40 percent. What is its approximate geometric growth rate? A: 10 minus 8 equals about 2 percent.

title: Arithmetic versus geometric mean return
one_line: The mean of terminal wealth grows at the arithmetic rate while the median grows at the geometric rate, so a positive expected return can sit on top of a typical path that loses money.
check: Q: A coin multiplies wealth by 1.5 or 0.6. After 100 flips what are mean and median wealth? A: 131 times and 0.0052 times, with 86.4 percent of players ending below where they started.

title: Utility function
one_line: A utility function is an invented ruler converting one number, the portfolio return, into a score, and only its shape matters because any positive affine rescaling leaves every decision unchanged.
sources: Four Numbers and What They Threw Away (https://claude.ai/code/artifact/0b20a92e-dc03-4b4c-aa3e-0a8a0c320608)
check: Q: What does u actually take as its argument in max E[u(w transpose R)]? A: The single scalar w transpose R, the portfolio's return; it never sees the weights or the individual stocks.

title: Concavity is risk aversion
one_line: A concave utility means each extra gain is worth less than the last, so losing five percent costs more than winning five percent gains, and that asymmetry is risk aversion restated.
sources: Four Numbers and What They Threw Away (https://claude.ai/code/artifact/0b20a92e-dc03-4b4c-aa3e-0a8a0c320608)
check: Q: On u = sqrt(1+r) at zero, compare the gain from plus 5 percent with the loss from minus 5 percent. A: 0.02470 gained against 0.02532 lost, so the loss is larger.

title: Certainty equivalent
one_line: The certainty equivalent is the guaranteed amount that scores the same as a gamble, and it sits below the gamble's mean for any concave utility by Jensen's inequality.
sources: Four Numbers and What They Threw Away (https://claude.ai/code/artifact/0b20a92e-dc03-4b4c-aa3e-0a8a0c320608)
check: Q: A coin flip between 0 and 200 dollars scored on sqrt(money) has what certainty equivalent? A: Fifty dollars, so this person swaps a fair flip on 100 dollars for 50 in cash.

title: Risk premium
one_line: The risk premium is the gamble's mean minus its certainty equivalent, the money handed over to make uncertainty go away, and it is the Jensen gap read along the horizontal axis instead of the vertical one.
sources: Four Numbers and What They Threw Away (https://claude.ai/code/artifact/0b20a92e-dc03-4b4c-aa3e-0a8a0c320608)
check: Q: For small gambles what is the closed form of the risk premium? A: About half the Arrow-Pratt coefficient times the variance, which contains no skewness or kurtosis at all.

title: Arrow-Pratt absolute risk aversion
one_line: The Arrow-Pratt coefficient is minus the second derivative over the first derivative of utility, and it multiplies half the variance to give the risk premium of a small gamble.
check: Q: Which 1964 paper derived this, and which one is usually misattributed? A: Pratt 1964 derived it, independently with Arrow; Sharpe 1964 is CAPM and Markowitz proposed mean variance in 1952.

title: Relative risk aversion
one_line: Relative risk aversion is wealth times absolute risk aversion, and it governs what fraction of wealth is put at risk rather than how many dollars.
sources: Four Numbers and What They Threw Away (https://claude.ai/code/artifact/0b20a92e-dc03-4b4c-aa3e-0a8a0c320608)
check: Q: Which quantity is constant for log utility, and what does that predict? A: Relative risk aversion, so the investor risks the same percentage of wealth at any size.

title: CARA CRRA and log utility
one_line: The three utility families named in the chapter differ only in which measure of risk aversion is constant, and therefore in how they treat ruin rather than in how they look near today's wealth.
sources: Four Numbers and What They Threw Away (https://claude.ai/code/artifact/0b20a92e-dc03-4b4c-aa3e-0a8a0c320608)
check: Q: Which of the three refuses any positive probability of ruin at any price, and why? A: Log utility, because it falls to minus infinity at zero wealth while CARA stays finite there.

title: Mean-variance is a truncated expansion
one_line: Cutting the Taylor expansion of expected utility after the quadratic term produces mean minus a multiple of variance, so mean variance optimisation is forced by the truncation rather than chosen as a convention.
sources: Four Numbers and What They Threw Away (https://claude.ai/code/artifact/0b20a92e-dc03-4b4c-aa3e-0a8a0c320608)
check: Q: Why is the risk term a variance and not a standard deviation? A: A second order expansion produces a squared deviation and nothing else, so the form is forced.

title: The skewness blind spot
one_line: Truncating after the second moment deletes the third derivative term, so every object downstream is blind to skewness by construction rather than by approximation error.
check: Q: Three books share mean 8 percent, volatility 15 percent and Sharpe 0.533. What separates their worst one percent of years? A: Minus 6.92 percent against minus 61.21 percent, a factor of 8.8 that no second moment metric can see.

title: Risk aversion parameter lambda
one_line: The lambda in an optimizer objective is the book's b over a ratio doubled, so it is the curvature of a utility function, and it changes only the size of the book and never its direction.
sources: Four Numbers and What They Threw Away (https://claude.ai/code/artifact/0b20a92e-dc03-4b4c-aa3e-0a8a0c320608)
check: Q: Solve max E[r] minus lambda over 2 times Var(r) with no constraints. What is w? A: One over lambda times Sigma inverse alpha, so lambda divides every weight and cannot rotate the portfolio.

title: Volatility as a risk measure
one_line: Volatility is defended not as the right description of risk but as the highest moment that can actually be estimated, since with a tail index between two and five nothing above the second is reliable.
sources: Four Numbers and What They Threw Away (https://claude.ai/code/artifact/0b20a92e-dc03-4b4c-aa3e-0a8a0c320608)
check: Q: State the two thresholds the footnote separates. A: A tail index above 2 to have a variance, and above 4 to estimate it consistently; existence and estimability are different questions.

title: Expected return of a strategy
one_line: Expected return is profit divided by assets under management, a division that buys comparability across periods because it is stationary and across funds because it is intensive.
sources: Four Numbers and What They Threw Away (https://claude.ai/code/artifact/0b20a92e-dc03-4b4c-aa3e-0a8a0c320608)
check: Q: Which word buys comparability across time and which across size? A: Stationary across time and intensive across size; dollar profit fails both at once.

title: Sharpe ratio
one_line: The Sharpe ratio divides expected excess return by volatility over the same horizon, collapsing the risk return plane into a single scalar an optimizer can climb, geometrically the slope of a ray through the origin.
sources: Four Numbers and What They Threw Away (https://claude.ai/code/artifact/0b20a92e-dc03-4b4c-aa3e-0a8a0c320608)
check: Q: What does a slope through the origin structurally fail to see? A: How far along the ray you are, which is the entire hole that capacity exists to fill.

title: Sharpe ratio as a t-statistic
one_line: Under iid returns the per period Sharpe ratio times the square root of the number of periods is exactly the t-statistic on the claim that the strategy makes money.
sources: Four Numbers and What They Threw Away (https://claude.ai/code/artifact/0b20a92e-dc03-4b4c-aa3e-0a8a0c320608)
check: Q: How long must a true annual Sharpe of 1.0 run to clear a t of 1.96? A: 3.8 years; at 0.5 it takes 15.4 years and at 0.3 about forty three.

title: Dimension of the Sharpe ratio
one_line: Return scales with the horizon and volatility with its square root, so the Sharpe ratio carries dimension one over the square root of time and is not a pure number.
sources: Four Numbers and What They Threw Away (https://claude.ai/code/artifact/0b20a92e-dc03-4b4c-aa3e-0a8a0c320608)
check: Q: One strategy is honestly 0.055 daily. What is it annually? A: 0.055 times the square root of 251, about 0.864, and neither figure is more true than the other.

title: Standard error of the Sharpe ratio
one_line: The standard error of an estimated Sharpe ratio is the root of one plus half its square, over T, so the extra term is the price of estimating the volatility too.
depends_on: Standard error of a sample mean
sources: Four Numbers and What They Threw Away (https://claude.ai/code/artifact/0b20a92e-dc03-4b4c-aa3e-0a8a0c320608)
check: Q: What multiplier does estimating the volatility from the same sample cost at SR 3? A: 2.35 times, against 1.22 times at SR 1, so excellence is harder to measure than mediocrity.

title: Autocorrelation inflation of the Sharpe ratio
one_line: Positive autocorrelation makes the variance of a sum exceed the sum of variances, so naive annualisation divides by too small a volatility and overstates the Sharpe ratio.
sources: Four Numbers and What They Threw Away (https://claude.ai/code/artifact/0b20a92e-dc03-4b4c-aa3e-0a8a0c320608)
check: Q: A fund reports Sharpe 2.78 with lag one autocorrelation 0.80 on a strategy whose true ratio is 0.90. What is the diagnosis? A: Smoothed marks; the fund is reporting one number twice.

title: Sharpe ratio sign inversion
one_line: Below zero the same division that penalises risk rewards it, so among losing strategies the Sharpe ratio prefers the one that took twice the risk to lose the same amount.
sources: Four Numbers and What They Threw Away (https://claude.ai/code/artifact/0b20a92e-dc03-4b4c-aa3e-0a8a0c320608)
check: Q: Compare minus 5 percent at 5 percent volatility with minus 5 percent at 10 percent. A: minus 1.00 against minus 0.50, and the riskier book scores higher.

title: Information ratio
one_line: The information ratio is the Sharpe ratio computed on idiosyncratic returns alone, so it scores stock selection after the factor component that any index fund would also have earned is removed.
sources: Four Numbers and What They Threw Away (https://claude.ai/code/artifact/0b20a92e-dc03-4b4c-aa3e-0a8a0c320608)
check: Q: A book with beta 1.15 scored Sharpe 0.49 on total return. What did it score on the idiosyncratic part? A: An information ratio of 3.04, six times higher, from the same trader and the same year.

title: Capacity
one_line: Capacity is the largest expected profit a strategy can produce subject to a floor on its Sharpe ratio, and it exists as a separate metric because the Sharpe ratio falls as size grows.
sources: Four Numbers and What They Threw Away (https://claude.ai/code/artifact/0b20a92e-dc03-4b4c-aa3e-0a8a0c320608)
check: Q: Why does capacity change with the floor you set? A: The same strategy peaks at 194 million dollars unconstrained and 177 million at a Sharpe floor of 1.0, so a capacity quoted without its floor is empty.

title: Value at risk and conditional value at risk
one_line: Value at risk is the loss exceeded with a given small probability and conditional value at risk is the average loss beyond it, so the second reads the shape of the tail rather than a single point on it.
sources: Four Numbers and What They Threw Away (https://claude.ai/code/artifact/0b20a92e-dc03-4b4c-aa3e-0a8a0c320608)
check: Q: Three books share mean, volatility and Sharpe ratio. What did their 95 percent CVaR run from? A: 14.6 percent to 21.5 percent, so the skewed book is 47 percent worse in the tail at an identical score.

title: Geometric Brownian motion
one_line: Geometric Brownian motion assumes constant volatility, Gaussian log returns and independent increments, and it is contradicted by every one of the four stylized facts, so it is a pricing model and never a risk model.
check: Q: Why does the wrong model survive? A: It is the unique process under which continuous delta hedging is exact, so it is constitutive for derivative pricing while being void for risk.

title: GARCH(1,1)
one_line: GARCH makes conditional variance a state with its own recursion, alpha times yesterday's squared return plus beta times yesterday's variance plus a constant, so it has no memory in the sign and long memory in the size.
sources: Three Roads to One Hidden Number (https://claude.ai/code/artifact/7933d34c-7c45-4c12-9671-be94ddc9d9a7)
check: Q: Which stylized fact does GARCH(1,1) with Gaussian innovations fail outright? A: Aggregational Gaussianity: aggregated GARCH is GARCH, still at kurtosis 6.51 at monthly frequency against 3.09 for an independent series.

title: Persistence and half-life
one_line: The sum of the GARCH reactivity and memory parameters is the persistence, and it alone sets the decay rate, so the half-life is the number worth arguing about rather than the parameters.
sources: Three Roads to One Hidden Number (https://claude.ai/code/artifact/7933d34c-7c45-4c12-9671-be94ddc9d9a7)
check: Q: Half-lives at persistence 0.97, 0.99 and 0.995? A: 23, 69 and 138 days, so a change in the third decimal doubles your risk model's memory.

title: IGARCH
one_line: Setting the offset to zero and forcing the two parameters to sum to one makes GARCH identical to an EWMA, a process with no long run variance whose multi day forecast is flat forever.
sources: Three Roads to One Hidden Number (https://claude.ai/code/artifact/7933d34c-7c45-4c12-9671-be94ddc9d9a7)
check: Q: Told that volatility is 3 percent today, what do GARCH and EWMA forecast a quarter ahead? A: GARCH decays to 1.85 percent and EWMA stays at 3 percent, because a random walk's best forecast is its current value.

title: Realized volatility
one_line: Realized volatility measures variance arithmetically from intraday squared returns instead of modelling it, and its relative error falls like the square root of two over the number of samples.
sources: Three Roads to One Hidden Number (https://claude.ai/code/artifact/7933d34c-7c45-4c12-9671-be94ddc9d9a7)
check: Q: Subdividing the day drives which standard error to zero and which not at all? A: The variance error falls like one over the root of n while the drift error is exactly flat, which is a theorem rather than a sample size problem.

title: Roll model
one_line: The Roll model writes the printed price as a latent random walk efficient price plus transient microstructure noise, which manufactures a negative autocorrelation of exactly minus the noise variance at lag one and zero beyond.
check: Q: What can you recover from closing prices alone under the Roll model? A: The effective spread, as twice the square root of minus the lag one autocovariance, with no order book data.

title: Volatility signature plot
one_line: Because microstructure noise adds a constant per observation, realized variance grows linearly in the sampling frequency, so sampling faster eventually measures the spread rather than the volatility.
sources: Three Roads to One Hidden Number (https://claude.ai/code/artifact/7933d34c-7c45-4c12-9671-be94ddc9d9a7)
check: Q: Why is five minute sampling the industry convention? A: It is the elbow of the signature curve, slow enough that the noise term is small and fast enough to beat down sampling error.

title: Harvey-Shephard model
one_line: Taking logs of squared returns turns a genuinely stochastic volatility model into a linear Gaussian state-space model with positivity for free, at the price of an observation noise of standard deviation 2.22 in log units.
sources: Three Roads to One Hidden Number (https://claude.ai/code/artifact/7933d34c-7c45-4c12-9671-be94ddc9d9a7)
check: Q: How large is the observation noise relative to the signal? A: The noise standard deviation of 2.22 log units exceeds the roughly 1.5 log unit range of equity log variance over a whole cycle.

title: Factor model
one_line: The factor model writes the cross-section of returns as alpha plus a loadings matrix times a short vector of factor returns plus idiosyncratic noise, which is first a parameter counting argument and only second a story about markets.
check: Q: Name the three assumptions on the residual and which one is known to be false. A: Independent of the factors, zero mean, and diagonal covariance; the third is false in practice and is patched by push-outs.

title: Parameter counting argument
one_line: An unrestricted covariance needs n(n+1)/2 numbers which grows quadratically, while a factor structure needs nm plus m(m+1)/2 plus n which grows linearly, so the data per parameter never catches up.
check: Q: At 3000 stocks and ten years of daily data, how many observations per parameter does each approach give? A: 1.67 unrestricted against 40.6 with sixty factors.

title: Loadings matrix
one_line: The loadings matrix is a tall thin store of how much each factor transfers into each asset, and its blocks are typically a market intercept column, country and industry dummies, and continuous style columns.
check: Q: Read a row of B and read a column. What is each? A: A row is one stock's complete description, a column is one factor's footprint across the whole market.

title: Factor returns
one_line: Factor returns are the short vector of per period returns to each factor, unobservable and inferred, and they are what a fundamental model produces afresh from one regression on every single date.
check: Q: Which of loadings and factor returns can you look up? A: The loadings; nobody publishes the return to value on Tuesday, so it has to be inferred.

title: Idiosyncratic returns
one_line: Idiosyncratic returns are what the factors did not account for, readable positively as asset specific news and negatively as a residue whose content changes whenever you add a factor.
check: Q: Give the two readings and say why the difference matters. A: A real economic object versus a leftover defined by subtraction; the second reading is why adding a factor silently changes what epsilon is.

title: Factor covariance identity
one_line: The return covariance equals B times the factor covariance times B transpose plus the idiosyncratic covariance, an exact identity in which alpha does not appear at all.
check: Q: Why is alpha invisible to the risk model? A: Covariance ignores constants, so shifting returns by a fixed vector does not change how they vary.

title: Alpha spanned
one_line: The component of alpha lying in the column space of the loadings is indistinguishable from factor expected returns, because a constant added to every period's factor return produces identical data.
check: Q: A researcher claims alpha in a direction the firm's risk model already spans. What are they claiming? A: A factor premium, definitionally, whatever the backtest says.

title: Alpha orthogonal
one_line: The component of alpha perpendicular to every loading column defines a portfolio whose factor exposure is annihilated exactly, so it earns the length of that vector with only idiosyncratic risk left.
check: Q: A unit portfolio along alpha orthogonal has what mean and what factor exposure? A: Mean equal to the norm of alpha orthogonal, and factor exposure exactly zero on every day and every realisation.

title: Root n Sharpe bound
one_line: Bounding the variance by the operator norm and the length by the one norm inequality gives a Sharpe ratio of at least the root of n times the per asset edge.
depends_on: One norm versus two norm inequality
check: Q: With a 1.2 basis point daily per asset edge and 40 percent maximum idiosyncratic volatility, what floor does the bound give at 10,000 names? A: An annualised Sharpe of 7.56, which no fund attains, so the per asset edge must decay.

title: Rotational indeterminacy
one_line: Replacing B by B C inverse and f by C f leaves every prediction unchanged for any invertible C, so a factor model identifies a subspace and never a particular basis.
check: Q: What is invariant under a rotation and what is not? A: Total factor variance and every prediction are invariant; per factor exposures and per factor risk shares are not.

title: Identity factor covariance rotation
one_line: Taking C from the SVD of the factor covariance makes the rotated factor covariance the identity, so portfolio factor variance becomes a plain sum of squared exposures with no cross terms.
check: Q: What does this rotation buy the risk manager? A: Exposures read directly as factor volatilities and risk becomes Pythagoras rather than a quadratic form full of covariances.

title: Orthonormal loadings rotation
one_line: Taking C from the SVD of the loadings makes B transpose B the identity, so the projection collapses to B B transpose and fitting factor returns needs no inverse at all.
check: Q: Can you have both an identity factor covariance and orthonormal loadings? A: No; twelve symmetric conditions on nine free numbers, and after the first rotation the eigenvalues of B transpose B are not all one.

title: Centring factor loadings
one_line: Scaling loadings is always a rotation but centring them is a shift, so it is only possible when the all ones vector lies in the column space, and then not on the very columns that build it.
check: Q: Why does centring every column make the rotation singular? A: The shift on the columns building the ones vector is exactly their own mean, so nu transpose a equals minus one and the determinant is zero.

title: Factor model projection
one_line: A projection replaces the loadings by a matrix whose range sits inside the original, choosing the factor returns that minimise the squared distance between the two systematic returns.
check: Q: Does a projected model necessarily report less risk than its parent? A: No; on the worked example factor variance rose 0.12 percent, because the criterion is pathwise closeness rather than portfolio variance.

title: Push-out
one_line: A push-out promotes structure out of the residual into new factors, and the new loadings must be orthogonal to the old ones or every original factor silently changes meaning.
check: Q: What happens if you add a non orthogonal factor? A: Returns stay identical to 6.9e-18 while the market factor's reported daily return moves by 38 basis points, purely from re dividing credit.

title: Performance attribution
one_line: Portfolio profit splits exactly into exposures times factor returns plus weights times idiosyncratic returns, and the same double sum can be regrouped by factor or by stock without changing the total.
check: Q: A twelve name book lost 188,151 dollars in a day. How did it split? A: minus 169,511 to factors and minus 18,640 idiosyncratic, so a good stock picker still had that day.

title: Factor exposures of a portfolio
one_line: The exposure vector b equals B transpose w, which turns n positions meeting n returns into m exposures meeting m factor returns, and it is an automatic consequence of holding the names.
check: Q: Why can a long in a low value stock and a short in a high value stock add to the same value exposure? A: Because both the characteristics and the weights can be negative, so their product has one sign.

title: Percentage idiosyncratic variance
one_line: Factor variance and idiosyncratic variance add to total variance and their percentages sum to one hundred, but the corresponding volatilities do not add because they are the legs of a right triangle.
check: Q: Adding factor and idiosyncratic volatility gave 322,726 dollars against a true total of 229,986. By how much does that overstate risk? A: Forty percent.

title: Marginal contribution to risk
one_line: The marginal contribution of a group is the change in portfolio volatility per unit of that group's volatility added, and it evaluates exactly to the correlation of the group's profit with the total.
check: Q: What free sanity check does that identity hand a risk system? A: Every marginal contribution must lie between minus one and one, because it is a correlation.

title: Share of variance as a beta
one_line: A group's share of portfolio variance collapses to the beta of that group's profit against the total profit, which is why the shares sum to one and why a share can legitimately be negative.
check: Q: When is a share of variance negative and what does it mean? A: When the group's profit is negatively correlated with the total, so that group is reducing risk.

title: Sharpe sensitivity rule
one_line: Adding risk to a group improves total Sharpe exactly when the group's own Sharpe exceeds its marginal contribution to risk times the total Sharpe, so the hurdle rises with how much the group duplicates what you already own.
check: Q: Value had the highest standalone Sharpe of five groups and still failed. Why? A: Its marginal contribution of 0.892 made it nearly the book itself, so its hurdle of 0.0446 exceeded its 0.0439.

title: Precision matrix
one_line: The optimizer consumes the inverse covariance rather than the covariance, and inversion sends every eigenvalue to its reciprocal, so the least reliably estimated small directions dominate the answer.
check: Q: A ten percent error on the smallest eigenvalue changes the matrix by 0.0005 percent. What does it change the inverse by? A: 3.25 percent, an amplification of about 6150 times.

title: Empirical covariance rank deficiency
one_line: With fewer days than assets the sample covariance has a large null space, so a majority of independent portfolios are assigned exactly zero volatility and an optimizer will take unbounded positions in them.
check: Q: With 200 assets and 60 days, one null space portfolio had estimated variance 4.2e-20. What was its true daily volatility? A: 1.87 percent, and the estimator is equally confident about 139 others.

title: Characteristic factor model
one_line: A characteristic model takes returns and firm characteristics as primitives and estimates factor and idiosyncratic returns from them, which is the practitioner default because its factors were named before they were fitted.
check: Q: Which two of the six construction steps does the book decline to give a method for? A: Universe selection and loadings generation, both called art rather than science.

title: Statistical factor model
one_line: A statistical model takes only returns as primitive and estimates both loadings and factor returns, so it recovers a subspace rather than a basis and its factors carry no names.
check: Q: Why can a statistical model never recover B itself? A: Rotational indeterminacy means B and B C describe the same model, so only the column subspace is identified.

title: Cross-sectional regression
one_line: A fundamental model runs one regression across the assets on each date, producing a fresh vector of factor returns per day with no time-series information used at all.
check: Q: On a scatter of loading against return for one date, what is the factor return? A: The slope of the fitted line, and the vertical distances are that day's idiosyncratic returns.

title: Factor-mimicking portfolio
one_line: Because an estimated factor return is a fixed weighted sum of asset returns fixed before the day starts, it is literally the return of a holdable portfolio with unit exposure to one factor and none to any other.
check: Q: What is B transpose times the FMP matrix, and how well does it check? A: The identity, measured at 2.22e-16, so it is algebraic rather than approximate.

title: Estimation universe
one_line: The estimation universe must be tradeable, well priced and relevant, and tradeability matters because a factor-mimicking portfolio holds every name in it, so one untradeable name makes the factor untradeable.
check: Q: Why does shortening the model period shrink the universe? A: Names that cannot support a reliable price in a ten minute window drop out, so periodicity and universe cannot be chosen separately.

title: Loadings timestamp convention
one_line: The model needs loadings known at the start of the interval, while most vendors stamp them at the end, so using them as delivered leaks the return you are trying to explain into the loading.
check: Q: What is the most common way a factor backtest produces untradeable results? A: A one line off by one indexing error on the loading timestamp.

title: Rank-deficient loadings matrix
one_line: Industry dummies sum to a column of ones and so does the country column, so a real model's loadings matrix is exactly singular and the factor returns are not identified rather than merely imprecise.
check: Q: Slide along the null direction: the country return runs from minus 1.6 to plus 50.4 percent. How much do fitted returns move? A: At most 2.78e-17, so no statistical test can prefer one answer.

title: Identification constraint on factor returns
one_line: Adding a side constraint such as requiring the market weighted sum of industry factor returns to be zero picks one of the infinitely many perfect fits, at no cost in fit and with every factor kept.
check: Q: Does the constrained country return equal the market return? A: No; it is the market return purged of industry tilts, differing by the cap weighted style contribution plus the residual.

title: Factor return inflation
one_line: Measured factor variance equals true factor variance plus (B transpose Omega epsilon inverse B) inverse, because a factor-mimicking portfolio holds real stocks and so carries their idiosyncratic noise.
check: Q: Which factors does the inflation hurt most and why? A: The smallest, because the correction is about the same size for every factor, running from plus 39 percent on the weakest to plus 12 percent on the strongest.

title: Dynamic conditional correlation
one_line: DCC splits the factor covariance into time varying volatilities and a correlation matrix and estimates each with its own half-life, giving correlations the longer memory because they move more slowly than volatilities.
check: Q: Which half-life is longer and what belief does that encode? A: The correlation half-life, because a crisis doubles volatilities in days while correlation structure changes over years.

title: Short-term volatility updating
one_line: STVU adds a latent multiplier on the whole covariance driven by whether the model's own z-scored factor returns are the size it predicted, so a slow estimator can react fast without giving up its calm.
check: Q: Volatility tripled on day 120. How long did each estimator take to reach 90 percent of the new level? A: Over 180 days for a 126 day EWMA, 39 for a 21 day one, and 19 with STVU on the slow one.

title: Idiosyncratic covariance matrix
one_line: The idiosyncratic covariance should be diagonal or sparse because anything shared should have been a factor, and any visible structure in it is a factor the model is missing rather than an estimation nuisance.
