check: Q: What does the book recommend doing to this matrix as a sanity check? A: Look at it, because striking patterns can be read as factors that should be added to the model.

title: Correlation thresholding
one_line: Keeping a residual correlation only when it clears a threshold recovers clusters, and the right threshold is found by sweeping until the clusters are stable and interpretable rather than by a formula.
check: Q: Three planted clusters were recovered exactly over what range of threshold, and what did the theoretical value do? A: A plateau from 0.28 to 0.42, while the theoretical 0.16 sat below it and merged everything.

title: Winsorization of returns
one_line: Because a factor return is the return of a mimicking portfolio, clipping a genuinely large return reports a portfolio return the portfolio did not earn, so real jumps must be kept and only bad data removed.
check: Q: One asset in 200 reported plus 200 percent from a missed split. What did that do to a style factor return? A: It moved by minus 0.02627 against a true 0.0025, wrong by 10.5 times and with the sign flipped.

title: Factor zoo
one_line: The published factor set has expanded far beyond what any model needs, and the four standard objections are incomplete classification, testing in isolation, toy portfolio construction and reuse of the same data.
check: Q: Which of the four objections lets two researchers independently discover the same effect? A: Testing in isolation against a three factor benchmark, so neither controlled for the other.

title: Market factor
one_line: The market factor is the most pervasive column, taken either as the vector of ones or as regression betas to an index, and taking it as ones is exactly what makes centring possible and the matrix singular.
check: Q: What does an all ones market column do to the column space? A: It puts the ones vector inside it, which permits centring in chapter four and causes rank deficiency in chapter six.

title: Industry and country dummy factors
one_line: Industry and country loadings are zero one variables summing to one per asset, which is why every stock's industry cells reproduce the country column exactly and the matrix loses rank.
check: Q: Measured on a real shaped loadings matrix, what is the maximum gap between the industry row sum and the country entry? A: Exactly zero, not merely small.

title: Momentum factor
one_line: The momentum factor loads on trailing three to twelve month performance on the finding that past winners keep winning, and it reverses sign at horizons of a month or less.
check: Q: What happens to the sign at a one week horizon? A: It flips to reversal, and the effect is stronger the more recent the outperformance.

title: Liquidity factor
one_line: The liquidity factor says illiquid names outperform as compensation for risk borne during liquidity spirals, and it is loaded through a price impact measure computed from data you already have.
check: Q: What does the Amihud measure answer in one sentence? A: How far does this stock move per dollar that trades in it, averaged over a window.

title: Principal component analysis
one_line: PCA finds the directions of greatest portfolio variance, which are the eigenvectors of the covariance and equally the left singular vectors of the return matrix, so approximation and variance maximisation give the same answer.
check: Q: The Lagrange multiplier in the maximum variance problem turns out to be what? A: The objective itself, v transpose Sigma v, so you want the largest eigenvalue.

title: Probabilistic PCA
one_line: Maximising a Gaussian likelihood with equal idiosyncratic variances leaves the eigenvectors untouched, sets the idiosyncratic floor to the average discarded eigenvalue, and subtracts that average from every kept eigenvalue.
check: Q: What problem with plain truncated PCA does this fix? A: Singularity: the discarded directions get variance lambda bar instead of zero, so the matrix can be inverted.

title: Spiked covariance model
one_line: The spiked model asserts a spectrum in two pieces, a bulk pinned at one after normalisation and a few eigenvalues growing linearly in the number of assets, which is what lets PCA separate signal from noise at all.
check: Q: Why should spike eigenvalues grow like n? A: B transpose B is n times the average per asset loading second moment, which converges to a fixed matrix, so its eigenvalues scale with n.

title: Eigenvalue shrinkage
one_line: Since a sample eigenvalue above the threshold converges to lambda plus gamma, subtracting gamma recovers the population value, and this offset is optimal in operator norm on both the covariance and its inverse.
check: Q: Why does the rule carry a domain restriction at one plus the root of gamma? A: Below the threshold the map from population to sample eigenvalue is flat, and you cannot invert a function that is not injective.

title: Eigenvector tilt
one_line: Above the threshold the estimated eigenvector is recovered only at an angle whose cosine is one over the root of one plus c, so even a comfortably detectable factor is found in a rotated direction.
check: Q: At factor strength 4.0 with gamma 0.5, what was the cosine between estimated and true eigenvector? A: 0.8929, not 1, so the direction is tilted even when the eigenvalue is clearly separated.

title: Number of factors
one_line: How many factors to keep can be chosen by a spectral threshold, a scree elbow, a maximum eigenvalue gap or a penalised fit, and the four criteria routinely disagree with each other and with the truth.
check: Q: Which direction should you err in and by how much? A: Toward too many: on one test three too few cost 14.95 percent of realised excess risk while eight too many cost 3.36 percent.

title: Factor churn
one_line: When two eigenvalues are close, one extra day of data can swap them, so individual PCA loadings can turn over almost completely in a day even though the subspace they span barely moves.
check: Q: Which single use of a risk model does churn actually break? A: Performance attribution, because what factor three contributed has no stable answer if factor three was a different portfolio each day.

title: Procrustes rotation of loadings
one_line: Choosing at each rebuild the orthonormal rotation closest to yesterday's loadings has the closed form V U transpose from the SVD of the cross product, and it removes almost all churn while changing no forecast.
check: Q: What did the rotation cost on the worked panel? A: Nothing: mean squared turnover fell 99.4 percent while the covariance matrix changed by 4.2e-17.

title: Sign indeterminacy of a principal component
one_line: An eigenvector and its negative solve the same equation, so the sign a solver returns is a coin flip and any interpretation that turns on a sign needs a stateful convention fixed once and carried forward.
check: Q: Across 60 resamples the three components reversed on 48, 47 and 50 percent of runs. What fixed it? A: Requiring one chosen reference asset per component to load positively, which cut the rates to about zero.

title: Interpreting components by regression
one_line: Regressing a statistical loading column on characteristics you already understand tells you what the component is made of, and the same technique interprets any risk model in terms of another.
check: Q: The first component's centred R squared was 0.0104 and its uncentred one 0.8494. Why is that the finding rather than a failure? A: The component is nearly constant across assets, which is exactly what a market factor is.

title: Idiosyncratic normalisation of returns
one_line: Dividing every return by its idiosyncratic volatility manufactures the bulk at one that every spiked model result requires, and it concentrates the spectrum so fewer components carry the variance.
check: Q: How many components reached half the variance under the three normalisations on real Russell 3000 data? A: Thirty raw, twenty by total volatility and ten by idiosyncratic volatility.

title: Volatility proxy
one_line: Every volatility test grades a forecast against a stand-in because the true volatility is never observed, and a single squared return is an unbiased proxy whose noise is larger than the thing it measures.
check: Q: What are the noise to signal ratios of a squared return and of a 78 sample realized variance? A: 1.41 and 0.16, since they are the same chi-squared family at k equal to 1 and 78.

title: QLIKE
one_line: QLIKE scores a variance forecast by the ratio of realized to forecast variance minus its log minus one, which is the Gaussian negative log-likelihood up to constants and punishes over forecasting harder than under forecasting.
check: Q: At a 75 percent proportional miss, what does QLIKE charge each way? A: 0.6363 for over forecasting against 0.1904 for under forecasting, a ratio of 3.34.

title: MSE loss for variance forecasts
one_line: The MSE loss weights the squared relative miss by the forecast variance, is exactly symmetric in the ratio of realized to forecast variance, and like QLIKE is minimised at the true variance.
check: Q: What does MSE charge at a fifty percent miss in each direction? A: 0.2500 either side, exactly symmetric, unlike QLIKE's 0.1931 against 0.0945.

title: Rank robustness of a loss
one_line: A loss is rank robust when it orders two forecasts the same way against a noisy unbiased proxy as against the truth, a property of the function itself and therefore free to choose correctly.
check: Q: Where is mean squared error on the log of the variance minimised when fed a squared return? A: At 0.2816, about 28 percent of the true variance, so it systematically selects a model that understates risk.

title: Bias statistic
one_line: The Bias statistic is the standard deviation of returns standardised by their forecast volatility, so it checks whether the level is right on average and cannot see whether the model knows which days are dangerous.
check: Q: What does a Bias statistic of one mean, and what can it not distinguish? A: The level is right on average; it cannot separate a model that tracks the variation from a flat line at the right average.

title: QDIST
one_line: QDIST is the Gaussian negative log-likelihood of the whole return vector, so it needs no portfolio at all and its two terms trade off, one punishing a matrix that is too small and the other one that is too big.
check: Q: One model scores 0.76 lower than another in QDIST. What does that mean? A: It made the observed cross-section about e to the 0.76, roughly 2.1 times, more likely on a typical day.

title: Minimum-variance test of a covariance matrix
one_line: Building the lowest variance portfolio under a candidate matrix and measuring its realised variance can only do worse than the truth, with equality exactly when the candidate is proportional to the truth.
check: Q: What does the proof reduce the variance ratio to, and what closes it? A: E[xi] times E[1 over xi] over the mismatch ratios, closed by Jensen since 1 over x is convex.

title: Mahalanobis distance
one_line: Mahalanobis distance measures a return vector in units of the model's own uncertainty by multiplying by the inverse square root of the covariance, which turns the ellipse of returns into a circle.
check: Q: Why is the exponent a half rather than a whole? A: Because covariance eats the transform twice, so the matrix must square to Omega inverse, and a full inverse would cancel twice.

title: MALV
one_line: MALV is the variance across days of the Mahalanobis statistic divided by the number of assets, benchmarked against two over n, and it is deliberately blind to a pure scaling of the matrix.
check: Q: Multiplying a correct matrix by 100 improved MALV ten thousand fold. What single number gives the trick away? A: The mean of the statistic, which fell to 0.0100 when a correct model puts it at 1.

title: Predicted beta
one_line: The predicted beta of every asset to a reference portfolio is Omega w divided by w transpose Omega w, a forecast built entirely from the covariance matrix with no returns in it at all.
check: Q: A name realised beta 1.518 and a diagonal model predicted 3.244. What does the hedge leave on the book? A: It overshoots by 1.726 units, leaving 47 percent of the asset's own daily risk still there.

title: Model turnover
one_line: Model turnover measures how much the factor-mimicking portfolio recipe changes between rebuilds, since every change is a trade even when nothing about the manager's views moved.
check: Q: Two models fit the cross-section equally well but averaged Frobenius turnover 0.0709 and 0.0048. What is the cost gap at ten basis points a side? A: About 349 basis points a year, bought with no improvement in accuracy.

title: Coefficient of determination in a factor model
one_line: R squared cannot select a factor model, because there is no holdout when factor returns are re-estimated every period, because adding random columns always improves it, and because a sign flipping rotation preserves it while destroying the factor correlations.
check: Q: Two models had identical R squared to ten decimals and the same parameter count. What differed? A: The estimated factor correlations, whose largest entry collapsed from 0.4557 to 0.0127.

title: Slippage reserve
one_line: A slippage reserve is cash held back before the optimizer runs, equal to a spread toll plus an impact term plus a confidence multiple of the drift standard deviation of the trade vector.
check: Q: A trade whose plan aimed exactly at a cash floor missed it by 6,055 dollars. How large a draw was that? A: About 0.85 standard deviations, an entirely ordinary move against a flat 500 dollar cushion.

title: Share of stock
one_line: A share is a small identical ownership slice of a company, a legal claim on a real business cut thin enough to trade, and a market simply adds a standing crowd willing to take the other side at any moment.
check: Q: Apple is cut into roughly fifteen billion shares. What does owning one entitle you to? A: About one fifteen billionth of everything Apple is, including its future profits and any dividends.

title: Order book
one_line: The exchange keeps every standing limit order in one sorted list, buyers with the highest price on top and sellers with the lowest, so the book is a queue of promises rather than a chart of prices.
check: Q: Between trades, is there a single price? A: No; only two walls of standing offers and a gap, and the number on a screen is the last trade, already history.

title: Bid and ask
one_line: The best bid is the highest price any buyer is offering and the best ask the lowest price any seller will accept, and a trade happens only when a new order is willing to cross between them.
check: Q: Whether the next print is a buyer lifting the ask or a seller hitting the bid is close to what? A: A coin flip, which is why the printed price alternates even when nothing about the asset has changed.

title: Limit order
one_line: A limit order says trade with me only at my price or better, so it controls the price but not whether or when it trades, and that patience is the raw material the whole book is built from.
check: Q: What does a limit order give up in exchange for price control? A: Certainty of execution; it may sit all day and never trade at all.

title: Market order
one_line: A market order says trade now at whatever the standing prices are, so it guarantees execution and surrenders control of the price, which is exactly the impatience the spread charges for.
check: Q: Which order type pays the spread and which one earns it? A: The market order pays about half the spread; the resting limit order is the side being crossed.

title: Spread
one_line: The spread is the gap between the best bid and the best ask, and it exists because nobody in the book wants to trade at a loss, so it is the cost of demanding immediacy.
check: Q: Roughly how much of the spread do you pay by trading immediately? A: About half of it, measured against the mid, and nobody bills you because it is baked into the price you got.

title: Spread in basis points
one_line: Quoting the spread as ask minus bid over the mid times ten thousand makes it comparable across stocks at different prices, and it tracks liquidity and risk rather than the price level.
check: Q: A 329 dollar stock showed a 1.38 dollar gap and a 22 dollar stock a one cent gap. Which market is wider in basis points? A: The expensive one, at 41.9 bps against 4.6 bps.

title: Depth of the book
one_line: Depth is how many shares are resting at each price rung, and a thin book means the same order flow moves the price much further than it would on a deep one.
check: Q: A crash is often described as more selling than usual. What is the better description? A: The same selling into a book that had gotten far thinner.

title: Walking the ladder
one_line: A market order larger than the size resting at the best price consumes that rung and climbs to the next, so its average fill price is the share weighted average of every rung it ate.
check: Q: You market buy 1,000 shares with only 300 offered at the best ask. What decides your average price? A: The prices of the successive rungs your order consumed, which is a first taste of market impact.

title: Market maker
one_line: A market maker continuously posts both a bid and an ask on the same stock and earns the gap, running a shop rather than doing anyone a favour, and their competition is why spreads on liquid names are a penny.
check: Q: Who provides most of the resting liquidity in a book? A: Professional market makers quoting both sides at machine speed, undercutting each other for queue position.

title: Inventory risk
one_line: A maker who buys must hold the shares until an impatient buyer appears, so when a stock becomes volatile the maker protects itself the only way it can, by widening its spread and shrinking its quoted size.
check: Q: Why does the same stock have a wide thin market in a storm and a tight deep one on a calm afternoon? A: Inventory held through a volatile stretch is dangerous, so makers quote the storm rather than the average.

title: Market impact
one_line: Market impact is the price move you cause yourself by showing up with a large order, distinct from the spread you cross, and it is what makes the Sharpe ratio a decreasing function of size.
sources: Four Numbers and What They Threw Away (https://claude.ai/code/artifact/0b20a92e-dc03-4b4c-aa3e-0a8a0c320608)
check: Q: Why does leverage leave the Sharpe ratio unchanged while size does not? A: Leverage scales return and volatility equally, while size trades larger quantities of the same names and the impact eats the gross edge.

title: Square root law of market impact
one_line: The standard impact model scales the cost with volatility times the square root of participation times the traded amount, so it is a rounding error at tiny participation and dominant at large.
check: Q: Six buys each under 0.03 percent participation produced what total impact leg? A: About 326 dollars, negligible, but the same formula explodes once participation reaches a few percent of daily volume.

title: Liquidity
one_line: Liquidity is how much can trade without moving the price, read jointly from the depth of the book and the tightness of the spread, and it is what spreads actually track rather than price or volatility alone.
check: Q: The tightest spreads in a real sample sat on SPY and NVDA, one calm and one volatile. What do they share? A: They are the most heavily traded, so competition crushes the gap regardless of volatility.

title: Amihud illiquidity measure
one_line: The Amihud measure averages absolute return divided by dollar volume, answering how far a stock moves per dollar that trades in it, a price impact measure needing no order book data.
check: Q: What makes this measure standard despite its crudeness? A: It is computable entirely from daily data you already store, with no order book feed required.

title: Block order
one_line: Grouping the same stock across many client accounts into one order gives every account the same average fill price, and the fairness costs a delay between the moment a trade is priced and the moment it fills.
check: Q: What does the block buy and what does it cost? A: It buys fairness across accounts and costs time, in which prices wander away from the number the plan used.

title: Custodian
one_line: The custodian is the vault that actually holds the accounts, both shares and cash, and settles each trade after it matches, sitting downstream of the broker and the exchange.
check: Q: Name the pipeline from a trading decision to a settled position. A: Decision to broker to exchange and matching engine, then settlement at the custodian holding the account.

title: Circuit breaker
one_line: A market wide circuit breaker halts all trading for fifteen minutes when the index falls seven percent from the prior close, a safety valve for exactly the case where every book empties at once.
check: Q: How often did the circuit breaker fire in March 2020 against its whole prior history? A: Four times in ten days, against once in the previous 23 years.

title: Short selling
one_line: Shorting borrows shares, sells them now and buys them back later, so the loss if the price rises is unbounded because the position must eventually be closed at whatever the price then is.
check: Q: Why is a short position asymmetric in risk? A: The gain is capped at the full price falling to zero while the loss is unlimited on the upside.

title: Short squeeze
one_line: When short interest is crowded, a rising price forces shorts to buy to cap their losses, and buying to close a short is still buying, so the move feeds itself until the forcing stops.
check: Q: What ends a squeeze? A: The mechanical fuel being cut, as when brokers restricted buying in January 2021 and the price collapsed almost as fast as it rose.

title: GameStop squeeze
one_line: In January 2021 a stock trading near sixteen dollars printed an intraday high of 483 dollars because short interest exceeded the free float and forced covering fed on itself, with nothing to do with the business.
check: Q: What general mechanism does this episode illustrate? A: Forced flows, trades made because a position compelled them, which are price insensitive by definition.

title: Liquidity vacuum
one_line: When everyone demands immediacy at once and makers withdraw, the same order flow walks down an empty ladder, so the move is partly an illusion of price and often snaps back once liquidity returns.
check: Q: What is the signature of a liquidity vacuum on a chart? A: Extreme intraday range followed by a fast partial reversal, unlike an information move which stays.

title: COVID crash
one_line: Between February and March 2020 the S and P fell about 34 percent in five weeks, a blend of genuine repricing under enormous uncertainty and a dash for cash that emptied every book at once.
check: Q: What was SPY's worst single session of the episode? A: 2020-03-16, closing down 10.9 percent, one of four circuit breaker days in ten.

title: Information gap
one_line: New facts arriving all at once are repriced between the close and the next open, so the price teleports rather than sliding, and the move is permanent rather than reversed.
check: Q: Meta fell 26.4 percent on 2022-02-03. Could a trader have sold at 300 on the way down? A: No; it closed at 323 and opened near 245 with essentially no trading in between.

title: Volatility clustering
one_line: Large moves tend to be followed by large moves of either sign and small by small, so returns forget direction instantly and remember magnitude for months.
check: Q: Give the feedback mechanism in one chain. A: Uncertainty rises, makers widen and thin the book, the same flow moves price more, measured volatility rises, and makers thin further.

title: Heavy tails of equity returns
one_line: Equity returns have power law tails with a tail index near four, so the variance exists comfortably, its own standard error barely exists, and the shape of the tail cannot be measured at all.
sources: Four Numbers and What They Threw Away (https://claude.ai/code/artifact/0b20a92e-dc03-4b4c-aa3e-0a8a0c320608)
check: Q: Why did the book print bootstrap intervals rather than point estimates of kurtosis? A: One interval ran from 12.8 to 48.1, telling you the tails are heavy and that you cannot pin down how heavy.

title: Absence of return autocorrelation
one_line: Lagged autocorrelations of returns are small except at intraday scales where microstructure intrudes, but zero autocorrelation implies neither independence nor unpredictability.
check: Q: A daily cross-sectional forecast has an R squared under one percent. Why is that a business? A: Information ratio is roughly the information coefficient times the root of the number of independent bets, so 2 percent across 1,500 names 250 times a year works.

title: Aggregational Gaussianity
one_line: Aggregating returns over longer horizons makes their distribution closer to Gaussian, which tells you the fat tails came from a varying variance rather than from the innovations themselves.
check: Q: Simulated kurtosis ran 5.4 daily, 4.4 quarterly and 3.3 annual. What does the decay imply about the source of the tails? A: They are produced by something that averages out, namely variation in sigma, since sums of power tailed variables keep their index.

title: Intraday U-shape
one_line: Volatility and spreads are highest at the open, calm through midday and tightest just before the close, because overnight news is still being digested early and competition is fiercest late.
check: Q: Roughly how much tighter are spreads at the close than the open in published measurements? A: About four times, which is why disclosed methodologies concentrate trading in the closing window.

title: Square root of time scaling
one_line: Because variances add over uncorrelated periods, the typical distance a price has wandered grows with the square root of elapsed time, so most of the uncertainty you will face arrives early.
check: Q: At 1.2 percent a day over 252 days, what is the annual volatility and what would no cancellation give? A: About 19 percent against 302 percent, which is the whole difference between root T and T.

title: Satisficing versus optimising
one_line: To satisfice is to stop at the first option that is good enough, which needs no single scale, whereas to optimise you must first collapse every competing consideration into one number to maximise.
sources: Four Numbers and What They Threw Away (https://claude.ai/code/artifact/0b20a92e-dc03-4b4c-aa3e-0a8a0c320608)
check: Q: Why can an optimizer not be handed high return and low risk? A: That is two directions, not one, so there is no direction to climb until somebody collapses the pair into a scalar.

title: Efficient frontier
one_line: The efficient frontier is the upper left boundary of the achievable risk and return pairs, and every point on it is optimal for some tradeoff, so nothing in the data alone picks one.
sources: Four Numbers and What They Threw Away (https://claude.ai/code/artifact/0b20a92e-dc03-4b4c-aa3e-0a8a0c320608)
check: Q: In unconstrained active space the efficient set is what shape, and what is its slope? A: A straight ray whose slope is the information ratio, on which every lambda lands somewhere.

title: Objective and constraint interchangeability
one_line: Capping risk and charging for risk select the same portfolio, because the Lagrange multiplier on the constraint is exactly the price in the objective, and sweeping the price traces the whole frontier.
sources: Four Numbers and What They Threw Away (https://claude.ai/code/artifact/0b20a92e-dc03-4b4c-aa3e-0a8a0c320608)
check: Q: What practical statement follows from the one to one correspondence? A: A risk limit is a hidden opinion about price and a risk charge a hidden opinion about limits; you never escape choosing.

title: Lagrange multiplier as the optimised value
one_line: In the maximum variance problem the multiplier turns out to equal v transpose Sigma v, which is the objective itself, so the usually meaningless accounting device is the quantity being maximised.
check: Q: How do you see which eigenvector solves the maximum variance problem? A: Multiply the stationarity condition by v transpose, find lambda equals the objective, and take the largest eigenvalue.

title: Maximum variance portfolio problem
one_line: Maximising the variance of a unit norm portfolio has stationary points exactly at the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix, which is the second and equivalent definition of a principal component.
check: Q: Why is the norm constraint necessary and why does it always bind? A: Without it the variance is unbounded, and scaling up strictly increases a quadratic objective so the optimum sits on the boundary.

title: Best low rank approximation
one_line: Finding the closest rank m matrix is an optimisation over two unknown matrices that collapses to a rank constraint, and Eckart-Young gives it a closed form so nothing has to be searched.
check: Q: At rank four the truncated SVD left squared error 634.94 and a random rank four basis left 9172.56. What is the useful content of the theorem? A: Not that the SVD is good, but that the optimisation has a closed form answer.

title: Minimum-variance portfolio
one_line: Minimising w transpose Omega w subject to one linear constraint gives a portfolio pointing along Omega inverse times the constraint vector, so the answer depends on the inverse and is unchanged by scaling the matrix.
check: Q: Why is this test blind to a matrix that is uniformly the wrong size? A: Scaling the objective does not move its argmin, so a matrix overstating every risk by thirty percent produces exactly the same portfolio.

title: Orthogonal Procrustes problem
one_line: Finding the orthonormal matrix that brings one matrix closest to another reduces to maximising a trace, and the answer is V U transpose from the SVD of their cross product.
check: Q: Why does the objective collapse to a single trace? A: Two of the four expanded terms contain no X and the remaining two are equal, leaving trace(A X) to maximise.

title: Endogenous cost in a budget constraint
one_line: A cost term that depends on the solution being computed makes the constraint's right hand side move as the optimizer works, so the objective and the accounting can never reconcile and costs belong in the objective instead.
check: Q: What is the design rule that falls out? A: Solution dependent costs go in the objective and the cash constraint takes only precomputed constants, or the solver treats the cost as a pseudo return.
